moves.counterattack: The cookie holds only a session id now, but the server must look up each profile.
You split the profile over many Set-Cookie headers, but each cookie still goes with every request.
The profile cookie lasts longer, so more old data stays in every browser.
You tighten SameSite, so users are signed out inside partner sites, and the cookie is still large.

turns.modelAnswer: Cookies go with every request, and one cookie is usually at most 4KB. Keep only a session id in the cookie. The server looks up the profile. The cost: one lookup per request.
keyPoints: Cookies are sent with every request.
A cookie is usually at most 4KB.
Store a session id and look up the data on the server.

scenarios.name: The busy night
scenarios.problem: A TV advert brings many visitors tonight. Your shop runs on one web server.

turns.threat: Tonight one server must answer every visitor. It cannot handle that load.

moves.counterattack: A forward proxy works for clients, so your one server still gets every request.
You plan more servers behind one address, but nothing shares the requests between them yet.
You prepare a 503 page, but many visitors see it instead of the shop.
A reverse proxy shares the requests over three servers, but you pay for three servers.

turns.modelAnswer: Put a reverse proxy in front of several web servers. It sends each request to one of them, so they share the load. The cost: you run and pay for more servers.
keyPoints: A reverse proxy sits in front of the servers.
It shares the load across several servers.
More servers cost more to run.

turns.threat: The new servers have a new IP address, but some visitors still reach the old server.

moves.counterattack: You add a new subdomain, but visitors still type the old name.
You keep the old server running until old DNS answers expire, so you pay for both.
You add another new server, but visitors with the old address never reach it.
A forward proxy helps clients, so the old address still sends visitors to the old server.

turns.modelAnswer: Computers and DNS servers keep a domain's data for some time. Then it expires, and they fetch the new IP address. Keep the old server answering until then. The cost: you run both servers for a while.
keyPoints: DNS answers are kept for some time.
Old copies expire and are refreshed later.
Run the old server until the change has spread.

turns.threat: At the peak, all servers are full. New visitors wait and then see a timeout.

moves.counterattack: Visitors see a friendly 503 page with a retry time, but some of them leave.
You answer with a 4xx code, so visitors think they did something wrong.
You redirect visitors to a waiting page, so each one makes another request to busy servers.
A forward proxy works for clients, so the visitors still wait.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer with 503 Service Unavailable when the servers are overloaded. Send a friendly page with it, and a Retry-After header if you can. The cost: some visitors leave.
keyPoints: 503 means the server is overloaded or down for now.
Send a friendly page with the 503.
Retry-After says when to try again.

scenarios.name: The office network
scenarios.problem: Your team of 40 works in one office. The internet line is slow, and staff also work on trains.

turns.threat: Every laptop downloads the same large web pages and files again and again.

moves.counterattack: A reverse proxy protects servers, so the laptops still download everything.
The office proxy stores and forwards pages, but it is one more machine to run.
Requests share one connection now, but the same files still cross the line many times.
Lookups come from the cache, but the same large files still cross the line.

turns.modelAnswer: A forward proxy works for a group of clients. It stores and forwards pages, so the group uses less bandwidth. The cost: one more machine to run.
keyPoints: A forward proxy acts for the clients.
It stores and forwards pages for the group.
The proxy is one more machine to run.

turns.threat: A new app on the laptops sends Connection: close, so each request needs a new TCP handshake.

moves.counterattack: Lookups come from the cache, but each request still waits for a new handshake.
A reverse proxy stands in front of servers, so the laptops still open new connections.
The app reuses open connections now, but idle connections still use server resources.

turns.modelAnswer: In HTTP/1.1, connections are persistent by default. Connection: close ends the connection after each response. Remove it, so requests reuse one connection. The cost: idle connections still use resources.
keyPoints: HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default.
Connection: close forces a new handshake each time.
Idle open connections still use resources.

turns.threat: Staff on the train use the app on a weak phone network. One lost packet stops every image.

moves.counterattack: HTTP/2 sends requests in parallel, but one lost TCP packet still blocks all streams.
The connection stays open, but a lost packet still blocks the images.
The office proxy cannot help staff on the train.
With HTTP/3 a lost packet blocks only its own stream, but your servers must support HTTP/3.

turns.modelAnswer: HTTP/2 runs over one TCP connection, so a lost packet can block all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. A lost packet then blocks only its own stream. The cost: your servers must support HTTP/3.
keyPoints: In HTTP/2, a lost TCP packet can block all streams.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
In QUIC, a lost packet blocks only its stream.

scenarios.name: Public Wi-Fi
scenarios.problem: Many customers shop on cafe and airport Wi-Fi. Someone on the same network may watch the traffic.

turns.threat: The sign-in page still works over plain http. An attacker on the Wi-Fi can read passwords.

moves.counterattack: Browsers ignore HSTS sent over plain http, so nothing changes.
Secure keeps the cookie off plain http, but the password still travels in plain text.
Every header and body now travel encrypted, but each new connection starts with a handshake.
You redirect to another http page, so the password is still in plain text.

turns.modelAnswer: Serve the sign-in page over HTTPS. The TLS handshake agrees on a secret key, and then every header and body is encrypted. The cost: each new connection begins with a handshake.
keyPoints: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
After the handshake, headers and bodies are encrypted.
Each new TLS connection starts with a handshake.

turns.threat: Customers who type http://shop.example.com reach the plain site first. An attacker can stop the switch to HTTPS.

moves.counterattack: Browsers now go straight to HTTPS until max-age ends, but the very first visit is still open.
The 301 to HTTPS works, but an attacker can still catch that first plain request.
You renew the certificate, but the first plain http request is still open.
Browsers upgrade images, but the page request itself is still plain http.

turns.modelAnswer: A 301 to HTTPS alone leaves the first plain request open. Also send Strict-Transport-Security over HTTPS with a long max-age. Later visits then use HTTPS directly. The cost: the first visit can still be attacked.
keyPoints: A 301 alone leaves the first request open.
HSTS makes the browser use HTTPS directly.
HSTS works only after one HTTPS visit.

turns.threat: A security review says the very first visit of a new customer is still open to attack.

moves.counterattack: TLS 1.3 is current, but the first plain http request is still open.
A longer max-age helps later visits, but the first visit is still open.
Your domain joins the preload list, but every subdomain must now work over HTTPS.

turns.modelAnswer: Join the HSTS preload list. Browsers then use HTTPS for your domain even on the first visit. The header needs a max-age of at least one year, includeSubDomains and preload. The cost: every subdomain must serve HTTPS.
keyPoints: Preloading protects the very first visit.
Preload needs a one-year max-age, includeSubDomains and preload.
Every subdomain must then work over HTTPS.

scenarios.name: The certificate warning
scenarios.problem: After a server move, some customers see a certificate warning. A few of them click through it.

turns.threat: The new server's certificate is for old.example.com, not for shop.example.com.

moves.counterattack: You turn on TLS 1.3, but the name on the certificate is still wrong.
You trace where the server proves its identity, but the name is still wrong.
The name points to the right IP address, but the certificate still names another site.
The new certificate names shop.example.com, but someone must keep it up to date.

turns.modelAnswer: A website certificate names the site it is for, and a CA signs it. The browser checks the name and the chain back to a root. Get a certificate for shop.example.com. The cost: someone must manage it.
keyPoints: The certificate must name the site.
The browser checks the chain back to a root certificate.
Someone must manage the certificate from now on.

turns.threat: Some customers still click through certificate warnings. An attacker could use a fake certificate the same way.

moves.counterattack: The right certificate is in place, but users can still click through a future warning.
Browsers stop click-through on certificate errors, but a broken certificate now stops every visitor.
Scripts over http are blocked, but users still click through the warning.

turns.modelAnswer: Send the HSTS header. For an HSTS host, the browser does not let users click through certificate errors. The cost: a broken certificate now stops every visitor.
keyPoints: HSTS blocks click-through on certificate errors.
Users can no longer accept a fake certificate.
A broken certificate now stops every visitor.

turns.threat: A scan shows the server still allows TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

moves.counterattack: You read the handshake steps, but the old versions are still allowed.
Only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are allowed now, so clients that know only old versions cannot connect.
You get a new certificate, but the old TLS versions are still on.
Preloading forces HTTPS, but the old TLS versions are still allowed.

turns.modelAnswer: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 should no longer be used. TLS 1.3 is the current version, and some sites still use 1.2. Turn off the old versions in the server config. The cost: clients that know only the old versions cannot connect.
keyPoints: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 should no longer be used.
TLS 1.3 is current, and 1.2 is still in use.
The server config decides the allowed versions.

scenarios.name: The broken menu
scenarios.problem: The shop moved to HTTPS. Now the menu does not work, and the browser console shows warnings.

turns.threat: The HTTPS page loads its menu script from http://cdn.example.com/menu.js.

moves.counterattack: You wait for the browser to upgrade it, but scripts are blocked, not upgraded.
The page itself is encrypted, but the browser still blocks the http script.
The script loads over HTTPS now, but you must find every other http script.
The CDN redirects http to https, but the browser blocks the http request first.

turns.modelAnswer: A script over http on an HTTPS page is blockable mixed content. Browsers block it, so the menu breaks. Load it over HTTPS. The cost: you must find every http link.
keyPoints: Scripts over http are blockable mixed content.
Browsers block them on HTTPS pages.
Every http link must change to https.

turns.threat: Product photos use img with src on http URLs. The team plans a week of photo fixes first.

moves.counterattack: You treat the photos as blocked, so the team spends a week on the wrong fix first.
The browser upgrades these photos itself, but photos from an IP address host are still blocked.
You check the certificate, but the photo links still use http.

turns.modelAnswer: Images set with src are upgradable. The browser requests them over HTTPS by itself. Fix the blocked scripts first. The cost: images from an IP address host are still blocked.
keyPoints: Images set with src are upgradable.
The browser asks for them over HTTPS itself.
Images from an IP address host are still blocked.

turns.threat: Visitors who type http://shop.example.com still get the old plain http pages.

moves.counterattack: Upgrades work only inside HTTPS pages, so the plain page stays plain.
You answer plain http with 403, so old links stop working.
The TLS versions are fine, but this visitor never starts TLS.
Plain http visits get a 301 to HTTPS, but each one costs an extra request.

turns.modelAnswer: Listen for plain http requests and answer 301 Moved Permanently to the HTTPS URL. The cost: one extra request on each plain visit. Add HSTS later to skip it.
keyPoints: Answer plain http with a 301 to HTTPS.
The Location header holds the https URL.
Each plain visit costs one extra request.

scenarios.name: The new blog
scenarios.problem: You launch a blog for the shop. It must be as safe as the shop itself.

turns.threat: Marketing says you must buy a new domain name before the blog can start.

moves.counterattack: The blog becomes blog.shop.example.com, but the new subdomain needs its own setup.
You test a lookup for a new name, but nobody has picked the name yet.
A reverse proxy can share the blog's load, but you still have no name for it.

turns.modelAnswer: Read a domain name from right to left. In shop.example.com, com is the TLD. You can create subdomains of a domain you control. The cost: the new subdomain needs its own setup.
keyPoints: Domain names are read from right to left.
You can create subdomains of a domain you control.
No new domain name is needed.

turns.threat: The shop sends HSTS, but blog.shop.example.com still loads over plain http.

moves.counterattack: You plan to preload, but the header needs includeSubDomains first.
Upgrades work only inside HTTPS pages, so the plain blog stays plain.
The header adds includeSubDomains next to max-age, but every subdomain must now support HTTPS.
The TLS versions are fine, but the blog still loads over plain http.

turns.modelAnswer: Add includeSubDomains to the shop's HSTS header. The rule then also covers blog.shop.example.com. The blog should send its own HSTS header too. The cost: every subdomain must support HTTPS.
keyPoints: includeSubDomains covers the names under the host.
Each subdomain should send its own HSTS header.
Every subdomain must then support HTTPS.

turns.threat: The blog shows the shop logo with img and has a form that posts to the shop. Security asks if this is allowed.

moves.counterattack: You see the blog is a different origin, but you do not know what is still allowed.
You change the cookie rules, but the question was about images and forms.
You plan a preflight check, but a plain form post does not need one.
The logo and the form keep working, but blog scripts still cannot read shop replies.

turns.modelAnswer: Cross-origin writes, like form posts, are typically allowed. Embedding, like img, is typically allowed too. Reads are typically blocked. The cost: blog scripts cannot read shop data without CORS.
keyPoints: Cross-origin form posts are typically allowed.
Embedding with img is typically allowed.
Cross-origin reads are typically blocked.

scenarios.name: The new front end
scenarios.problem: The new front end runs on https://app.example.com. It calls the API on https://api.example.com.

turns.threat: Every fetch() to the API fails, and the console says the read was blocked.

moves.counterattack: Both names end in example.com, but the policy compares the whole host.
You see the hosts differ, so the origins differ, and the API must now opt in.
You know cross-origin reads are blocked, but not yet why these calls are cross-origin.
You change SameSite, but the same-origin policy still blocks the read.

turns.modelAnswer: Content-Type: application/json makes the request not simple. So the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight.
